title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a positive integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Solve it with the prefix-sum remainder pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Subarray Sums Divisible by K (Prefix Remainder Counting)
keyPoints: Two prefix sums with the same remainder mod k bound a subarray divisible by k.
Track prefix-sum remainders in a frequency array of size k.
Normalize negative remainders with ((prefix % k) + k) % k to keep them in [0, k-1].
Seed remainder 0 with count 1 for the empty prefix.
Use an int[k] frequency array instead of a HashMap for speed when k is bounded.
Time is O(N) and space is O(k).

s1_definition.oneliner: Two prefix sums sharing the same remainder mod k bound a subarray divisible by k, so count equal-remainder pairs.
s1_definition.profdef:
- This problem counts subarrays whose sum is a **multiple of k**, in an array with possible negatives.
- A subarray sum is divisible by k when the **two bounding prefix sums share the same remainder** mod k.
- Track remainders in a **frequency array** of size k, incrementing at each step.
- **Normalize** negative remainders: `r = ((prefix % k) + k) % k`.
- **Seed** remainder 0 with count 1 for the empty prefix.
- Time is **O(N)** and space is **O(k)**.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews daily net cash flows and counts how many continuous stretches sum to an exact multiple of a settlement unit k (say multiples of 5000 rupees), because only multiples of the unit can be batched cleanly for the clearing house. He tracks the remainder of his running total and counts pairs of matching remainders.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem counts subarrays whose sum is divisible by k in an array with possible negatives, and you solve it in linear time with prefix sums reduced modulo k. The modular insight is that two prefix sums bounding a subarray yield a divisible sum exactly when they share the same remainder mod k. You scan once, keeping a running prefix and a frequency array of remainders, and at each index you add the count of earlier prefixes sharing the same remainder.

The correctness detail is remainder normalization. In Java, the percent operator can produce negative remainders, so you normalize with `((prefix % k) + k) % k` to keep remainders in `[0, k-1]`. Without this step, congruent prefixes of opposite sign land in different buckets and the count is wrong. Seed the remainder-zero bucket with 1 for the empty prefix.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the batch-settlement team. Daily net flows could only be grouped into a settlement batch if the total was an exact multiple of the clearing unit. The remainder-based counting gave all qualifying stretches in a single linear pass, and the normalization was essential because flows could be negative.

The senior-level insight is that this is the divisibility cousin of subarray-sum-equals-k, where you bucket by remainder instead of exact prefix value. The negative-remainder normalization is the single detail that distinguishes a correct implementation from a broken one.

Remember one sentence: two prefix sums with the same remainder mod k bound a divisible subarray; normalize negative remainders and count equal-remainder pairs.
